id="bfo6HfKIqfYWs8Ct_7uy-15" value="Example 3-D<div>&nbsp;Interface Interaction Graph</div>" style="text;html=1;align=center;verticalAlign=middle;whiteSpace=wrap;rounded=0;fontStyle=1" parent="1" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry x="225" y="30" width="170" height="30" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="bfo6HfKIqfYWs8Ct_7uy-16" value="A graph of 'interface structures as interacting spectrums'<span style="background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));">&nbsp;can identify missing graphs that are useful to identify, like how a 'function interaction map' can be identified as useful to connect to a 'structure similarity map' when the structure map is incomplete, which indicates comparing it to a more complete graph can identify missing components. This graph is also useful to describe why not all combinations of interface structures are useful, where primarily only the intersection points are useful/relevant/meaningful.</span><div><span style="background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));"><br></span></div><div><span style="background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));">For example, a graph indicating the attributes like 'chirality' of structures like 'substances' is likely to be incomplete and incapable of predicting 'future useful substances' on its own, because it leaves out context like other graphs like 'usage graphs (indicating how and where and why a substance is used, like whether its used in a particular pathway or organ)' and 'interactivity graphs (indicating probable interactions between bio system structures and substances like whether the substance can cross the blood-brain barrier, or substance-substance interactions)' and 'function maps (indicating how functions interact in the bio-system)' and 'causal variable graphs (indicating how structures can cause other structures)' as well as connections between these graphs. Similarly, 'graphs of structural similarities' can be too simple to identify structures like 'limits/thresholds' which differentiate very similar structures.</span></div>" id="bfo6HfKIqfYWs8Ct_7uy-72" value="With only the structural similarity graph, similar substances based on structure can be identified.<div><br></div><div>Once this is connected to a function map (connecting functions that interact with substances like 'substance-filtering', 'substance-activation', 'substance-binding', etc), information about the 'interaction profile' of a substance is identifiable, for example 'which substances bind with which receptors'.&nbsp;</div><div><br></div><div>As an alternate path to identifying binding affinity, connecting differences between the substance structural similarity graph and the bio-system structural similarity graph is useful to identify structures that are likely to bind.</div><div><br></div><div>Once this is connected to a causal variable graph, information about interactions between substances and causal sequences like 'processing pathways' can be identified, so that information about for example 'bio-availability of the substance' is identifiable.</div><div><br></div><div>This can be iterated with interface structures like 'combinations' to generate graphs like 'structure-function-intent graphs' to identify info like what a structure is useful for once it interacts with a function (like has a function or is input to a function).</div>" div.div:
A graph of 'interface structures as interacting spectrums' can identify missing graphs that are useful to identify, like how a 'function interaction map' can be identified as useful to connect to a 'structure similarity map' when the structure map is incomplete, which indicates comparing it to a more complete graph can identify missing components. This graph is also useful to describe why not all combinations of interface structures are useful, where primarily only the intersection points are useful/relevant/meaningful.
For example, a graph indicating the attributes like 'chirality' of structures like 'substances' is likely to be incomplete and incapable of predicting 'future useful substances' on its own, because it leaves out context like other graphs like 'usage graphs (indicating how and where and why a substance is used, like whether its used in a particular pathway or organ)' and 'interactivity graphs (indicating probable interactions between bio system structures and substances like whether the substance can cross the blood-brain barrier, or substance-substance interactions)' and 'function maps (indicating how functions interact in the bio-system)' and 'causal variable graphs (indicating how structures can cause other structures)' as well as connections between these graphs. Similarly, 'graphs of structural similarities' can be too simple to identify structures like 'limits/thresholds' which differentiate very similar structures.

div.div:
With only the structural similarity graph, similar substances based on structure can be identified.
Once this is connected to a function map (connecting functions that interact with substances like 'substance-filtering', 'substance-activation', 'substance-binding', etc), information about the 'interaction profile' of a substance is identifiable, for example 'which substances bind with which receptors'.
As an alternate path to identifying binding affinity, connecting differences between the substance structural similarity graph and the bio-system structural similarity graph is useful to identify structures that are likely to bind.
Once this is connected to a causal variable graph, information about interactions between substances and causal sequences like 'processing pathways' can be identified, so that information about for example 'bio-availability of the substance' is identifiable.
This can be iterated with interface structures like 'combinations' to generate graphs like 'structure-function-intent graphs' to identify info like what a structure is useful for once it interacts with a function (like has a function or is input to a function).

div.div:
Graph usefulness variants
There is always some way for a structure to be useful and useless on some variable/spectrum or on some other graph, but some graphs indicate this more optimally than others.
Identifying a graph that integrates all of these usefulness graphs is a useful intent

div.div:
This graph, taken from the intersecting spectrum graph, can be usefully varied to apply graph sequences, so that high volatility and low complexity graphs can be identified, for example.
It can also be usefully varied to apply cross-interface combinations like maximally different combinations, like sensitivity and specificity, to identify graphs with high sensitivity and specificity, for example.
Graphs that vary by these variables are useful to connect by this similarity, and its useful to connect graphs by intent relevance in graph sequences, and its useful to connect graphs by 'causality' for intents like 'evaluatability'.
